title: First to Worry, Last to Rejoice
text:
Fan Zhongyan was a Song dynasty statesman who rose from a poor childhood through the civil service examinations. In the early 1040s he led an ambitious program of government reforms, known as the Qingli Reforms, meant to curb favoritism and make officials more capable. Powerful opponents brought them down within about two years, and Fan and his allies were sent away from the capital to provincial posts.

In 1046 his friend Teng Zijing, who had also been demoted and posted to Yuezhou on Lake Dongting, rebuilt the famous Yueyang Tower there and asked Fan to write an essay to commemorate it.

Fan's short essay describes how visitors to the tower feel gloomy when the lake is dark with storms and joyful when it shines in spring sunshine. Then he turns to the people of old who were truly virtuous. They were not made happy by things or sad on their own account. In high office they worried about the people; far from court they worried about their ruler. Such people, he wrote, would be the first to worry about the world's troubles and the last to enjoy its pleasures.

The line became one of the best-known statements of the ideal of public service in China. Fan later used his own income to found a charitable estate supporting his clan.
lesson: A leader's place is to worry before others and to enjoy rewards after them. Ask whether your comforts come before or after your people's.
source: Fan Zhongyan, Record of Yueyang Tower (Yueyang Lou Ji), 1046
